correctness.rationale: The orthogonal splitting into constants, classwise zero-sum vectors, and class-constant global zero-sum vectors gives the diagonal resolvent at a vertex in class p as [1+Nt+(N-p)t²]/[(1+Nt)(1+(N-p)t)], t=θh. Subtraction for p>q gives the positive difference t(p-q)[1+(N-1)t]/[(1+Nt)(1+(N-p)t)(1+(N-q)t)]. The inverse is nonnegative: if (I+tL)x is nonnegative and x has a negative minimum at i, then [(I+tL)x]_i≤x_i<0. T=[R−(1−θ)I]/θ for θ>0, and T preserves constants. For finite h the diagonal resolvent is strictly above 1/N and tends to 1/N as h→∞; hence θ=1−1/N is included in the unbounded regime. Below that threshold, clearing positive denominators gives 1+Bh−Aθh²; the unique positive root for θ>0 is the stated radical. Euler gives the exact linear restriction and the same active classes, with equality allowed. The strict increase with s is in the finite-horizon regime, as in the proof, and the Crank–Nicolson specialization follows by substitution. At h=c/N the diagonal limit is 1/[1+θ(1−α)c], also for bounded s when α=0 since the nonconstant denominators coalesce. Bracketing the level 1−θ at two fixed c proves the scaled limit; Euler is direct. value.rationale: For a diffusion integrator the precise loss of nonnegativity matters, not just stability or a sufficient step bound. The structural result replaces a full-matrix positivity test on arbitrary multipartite profiles by two graph parameters, identifies exactly which vertices cause failure, and determines the large-N scaling under arbitrary admissible profiles. The general resolvent framework alone does not supply that graph-level reduction.
